body.text: In short:
Thousands across Australia have protested changes to insurance rules that advocates say will make it more difficult for people to homebirth.
An exemption allowing private midwives to attend homebirths without indemnity insurance will be scrapped in the new year.
Homebirth Australia has organised rallies at 26 locations across the country.
Families and advocates are warning of a "catastrophic collapse" in access to midwife-supported homebirths, as thousands rally across the country protesting new insurance rules.
From January 1, a longstanding exemption allowing privately practising midwives to attend homebirths without private indemnity insurance will be scrapped.
This means only a small percentage of Australia's midwives will be allowed to continue attending homebirths.

About 5 per cent of the country's 35,000 registered midwives are "endorsed" and allowed to obtain the necessary insurance, according to Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) Nursing and Midwifery Board data.
Advocacy organisation Homebirth Australia says the change will drive women and families into feeling forced to freebirth, or give birth at home without a midwife or medical practitioner.
Coordinator Katelyn Commerford said the insurance changes are particularly concerning for women in regional areas, who already face limited access to health services.
"Some women are choosing homebirths because their local hospital might be three hours drive away," she said.

"You've got women who are going to end up birthing on the side of the road of a national highway with trucks flying past them on the phone to a Triple Zero operator that's never even seen a birth before."
'Our bodies, our babies, our births'
Homebirth Australia has organised rallies at 26 locations across the country, including Sydney's Hyde Park, where hundreds of mothers, fathers and children attended.
Families chanted together, "Our bodies, our babies, our births," and called on the Federal Health Minister Mark Butler to ensure women continue to have access to safe homebirths.
Outside the Northern Territory's parliament house, hundreds gathered to protest the changes.
Darwin mother-to-be Jessica said she had been planning for months to have a home birth but would likely have to abandon her plans, and had been considering a freebirth.
"I understand the risks with it … but I [can't] pretend it hasn't crossed my mind," she said.
"That's how terrified I am of being forced to give birth at a hospital."
Endorsed midwife Helena Ruane called on the government to establish a working group to find a "permanent and affordable insurance solution".
"Today isn't simply about insurance … it's about human rights," Ms Ruane said.
Minister says insurance a 'no-brainer'
The temporary exemption allowing registered midwives to attend homebirths without indemnity insurance was first established in 2009.
In Australia, a planned homebirth legally requires two midwives — the first midwife must be endorsed, but that rule does not currently apply to the supporting second midwife.
Minister Butler said earlier this week it was a "no-brainer" that all health practitioners, including midwives, should need insurance.
"Particularly [when] delivering services like birthing, given the huge consequences in those rare circumstances where things go wrong," he told the ABC.

"An insurance product has now been developed and is offered to midwives, and as a result 18 months ago, health ministers across the country decided to bring midwives delivering home birthing services into line with every other health practitioner."
Better Births Illawarra co-founder Sharon Settecasse said the insurance on offer was not suitable for all midwives, and the rule change had dangerous implications.
"We're worried that babies and mothers are going to die if this exemption doesn't get extended," she said at a rally in Wollongong.
Australian College of Midwives President Ali Teate agreed the government had not developed an appropriate insurance policy.
"We want women to be able to access a midwife who has insurance," Dr Teate said at a rally in Glenelg, Adelaide.
"The solution is to stop the extra hoops that midwives need to jump through to get that insurance."
Queensland Nurses and Midwives Union Assistant Secretary Fridae King echoed that sentiment at a rally in Brisbane.
"The message today is that we need the government to come up with a reliable solution for insurance," she said.
Families warn of supply squeeze
Endorsed midwife Ciara O'Brien said she believed women should be able to give birth where they feel safest, and agreed the rule change may lead to dangerous births.

"Some women choose to make that choice, to birth alone, and that's absolutely their choice. The issue is when women are forced to make that choice because there's no other options for them," she said at a rally in Perth, where hundreds attended.
About 400 kilometres away in Geraldton, Cath Tan said she was the only privately practising endorsed midwife north of Perth offering homebirths.
"There's no access here at all … it's definitely not fair," she said.
Midwife Jaimee Shannon became emotional as she described the impact on women in Geraldton.
"I chose to be a midwife to give women a choice and be supported and heard, and this change is the complete opposite," she said.
"This change is ridiculous. Give us an exemption in regional and remote areas."
In the Riverina region, Wagga Wagga mother Marnie Butt said there were not enough endorsed midwives to support the amount of people wanting homebirths.
"We've only got two endorsed midwives here locally [so] their capacity fills really quickly," she said.
